slide_text: Backtracking — Exhaustive Search, Done Right Some problems have no formula. Nobody can compute the solution of a Sudoku puzzle — you have to try possibilities . The art is in trying them systematically: Enumerate — walk through every candidate, missing none, repeating none. Check — recognize a valid (or doomed) state quickly. Backtrack — when a choice leads to a dead end, undo it and try the next one. You already met this idea once: the wildcard in the Pattern Matching chapter tried both branches and gave up on the ones that failed. In this chapter you build the technique up from tiny exercises until you can solve any Sudoku board. Prerequisite: the Recursion chapter. Navigate: press or Space to advance | to go back

Challenge (skip ahead if you can): Write a Sudoku solver using backtracking. Given a 9×9 grid (a list of lists, with for empty cells), fill every empty cell so that each row, column, and 3×3 box contains the digits 1–9 exactly once. Try a digit, recurse, and undo it if it leads to a dead end. Return if the puzzle is solved (the grid is modified in place), or if no solution exists. [code block] [code block] Already got it? Quick Check 3.1 — Permutation Count How many permutations does a list of 4 distinct elements have? A. 4 B. 16 C. 24 D. 256 Answer: C. 4! = 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24. Each position has fewer choices than the last because you cannot reuse an element.

Part 4: Checking a State — Valid Parentheses Exhaustive search lives or dies by its checker — the little function that says "this state is fine" or "this state is broken". Before Sudoku, practice on brackets.

Before coding: as you scan left to right, you need to remember which openers are still waiting for their closers. What data structure naturally handles "most recent first"? Push openers onto it; when you see a closer, check the top of the stack. Hint 2 Create a dictionary mapping each closer to its opener: . When you see a closer, pop the stack and check whether the popped opener matches. If the stack is empty when you try to pop, the string is invalid. Solution [code block]

Quick Check 5.1 — Why Backtracking Prunes A 9×9 Sudoku has 81 cells. If you tried every possible assignment of digits 1–9 to all empty cells (brute force without checking constraints), approximately how many combinations would that be for a puzzle with 50 empty cells? A. 50 × 9 = 450 B. 9^50 — an astronomically large number C. 50! (50 factorial) D. 81 x 9 = 729 Answer: B. Each of the 50 empty cells can hold any of 9 digits, so brute force would try 9 x 9 x ... x 9 (50 times) = 9^50. Backtracking avoids almost all of these by pruning bad branches early.

Think — Why Is This Fast? The puzzle has 51 empty cells. Blind enumeration would try up to 9⁵¹ ≈ 10⁴⁸ boards — the sun would burn out first. Your solver finishes in well under a second. The difference is pruning : kills a bad branch at its first wrong digit, so the enormous tree of possibilities almost entirely never gets built. Enumeration provides completeness; checking provides the speed.
